questions.answer: $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ can donate a proton (to give $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$) or accept one (to give $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$).

questions.question:
Which of the following substances are structural isomers of each other?

I. $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3$

II. $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_3$

III. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
questions.answer: I and III are both $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$; II is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$.

Which is a conjugate acid–base pair in the following reaction?
$$\text{HNO}_3+\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{NO}_3^++\text{HSO}_4^-$$
questions.answer: The two members of a conjugate pair differ by one proton. Here $\text{HNO}_3$ acts as a base.

questions.question:
Consider $2\text{NO}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)$, $K_{eq}=0.01$. What happens when the volume of an equilibrium mixture is decreased at constant temperature?

I. The value of $K_{eq}$ increases

II. More $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ is formed

III. The ratio $\dfrac{[\text{NO}_2]}{[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]}$ decreases
questions.answer: The system shifts towards fewer gas moles, forming $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ and lowering the ratio. $K_{eq}$ depends only on temperature.

questions.question: For the Haber process, $\text{N}_2(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NH}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-92$ kJ mol⁻¹, temperature and pressure are chosen as a compromise between yield, rate and cost. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles but needs more costly equipment and energy.

A lower pressure would ensure a higher yield at a lower cost.
A lower temperature would ensure a higher yield and a faster rate.

questions.question: $K$ for $2\text{HI}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)$ is 0.25 at 440 °C. What is $K$ for $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$ at the same temperature?

questions.answer: Both contain the same moles of acid, so need the same volume of base; the initial and equivalence pH differ.

questions.question: At 25 °C, $K_{sp}$ values are: $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ $9.0\times10^{-12}$; $\text{BaCrO}_4$ $2.0\times10^{-10}$; $\text{PbCrO}_4$ $1.8\times10^{-14}$. Which chromate has the greatest molar solubility in water?
questions.answer: Molar solubilities: $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ $\sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}=1.3\times10^{-4}$; $\text{BaCrO}_4$ $1.4\times10^{-5}$; $\text{PbCrO}_4$ $1.3\times10^{-7}$ mol L⁻¹.
options: There is insufficient data to determine this

questions.question:
Iron(III) nitrate reacts reversibly with potassium thiocyanate:
$$\text{Fe(NO}_3)_3(aq)+3\text{KSCN}(aq)\rightleftharpoons3\text{KNO}_3(aq)+\text{Fe(SCN)}_3(aq)$$
Initially there was 0.250 mol of iron(III) nitrate and 0.500 mol of potassium thiocyanate in 100.00 mL of solution (no products). At equilibrium there was 0.100 mol of iron(III) thiocyanate. Calculate $K$ at this temperature.
questions.answer:
| mol L⁻¹ | $\text{Fe(NO}_3)_3$ | KSCN | $\text{KNO}_3$ | $\text{Fe(SCN)}_3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 2.50 | 5.00 | 0 | 0 |
| Change | −1.00 | −3.00 | +3.00 | +1.00 |
| Equilibrium | 1.50 | 2.00 | 3.00 | 1.00 |

$$K=\frac{[\text{KNO}_3]^3[\text{Fe(SCN)}_3]}{[\text{Fe(NO}_3)_3][\text{KSCN}]^3}=\frac{3.00^3\times1.00}{1.50\times2.00^3}=2.25$$

*Note: the answer follows the equation as the paper wrote it. In solution these salts are ionised and the real equilibrium is $\text{Fe}^{3+}+\text{SCN}^-\rightleftharpoons\text{FeSCN}^{2+}$.*

questions.question: The graph shows the concentrations of the three substances in $\text{PCl}_3(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{PCl}_5(g)$, $\Delta H=-92.5$ kJ mol⁻¹, over 14 minutes. Outline what is occurring between $t=3$ min and $t=5$ min.
questions.answer: The system is at dynamic equilibrium: the concentrations are constant because the forward and reverse reactions are occurring at equal rates.

questions.question: The graph shows the concentrations of the three substances in $\text{PCl}_3(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{PCl}_5(g)$, $\Delta H=-92.5$ kJ mol⁻¹, over 14 minutes. Calculate the equilibrium constant using the data at $t=4$ min.

The graph shows the concentrations of the three substances in $\text{PCl}_3(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{PCl}_5(g)$, $\Delta H=-92.5$ kJ mol⁻¹, over 14 minutes. Identify the stress that occurred at $t=8$ min and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The temperature was **increased**. At 8 min no concentration changes suddenly (ruling out adding or removing a species or changing volume); instead all three change gradually, with $[\text{PCl}_5]$ falling and $[\text{PCl}_3]$ and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ rising, so the equilibrium shifted left. The forward reaction is exothermic, and by Le Chatelier's principle heating favours the endothermic reverse reaction, which absorbs some of the added heat.

questions.question: The graph shows the concentrations of the three substances in $\text{PCl}_3(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{PCl}_5(g)$, $\Delta H=-92.5$ kJ mol⁻¹, over 14 minutes. At $t=8$ min the temperature of the system was increased. Explain the resulting shift in terms of collision theory.
questions.answer:
At a higher temperature particles move faster, collide more often and a greater proportion have energy at least equal to the activation energy, so both rates increase.

The endothermic reverse reaction has the larger activation energy, so the proportion of particles able to react increases by a greater factor for it. The reverse rate becomes greater than the forward rate and there is a net shift to the reactants until the rates are equal again.

questions.question: The solubility product of barium hydroxide at 25 °C is $K_{sp}=2.55\times10^{-4}$. Calculate the molar solubility of barium hydroxide at 25 °C.
questions.answer:
$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ba}^{2+}+2\text{OH}^-$ gives $K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3$.

$$s=\sqrt[3]{\frac{2.55\times10^{-4}}{4}}=3.99\times10^{-2}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question: The solubility product of barium hydroxide at 25 °C is $K_{sp}=2.55\times10^{-4}$. Calculate the molar solubility of barium hydroxide in a 0.150 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide solution at 25 °C.
questions.answer:
$K_{sp}=s(0.150+2s)^2=2.55\times10^{-4}$.

Solving numerically (successive approximation) gives $s\approx9.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

*Note: the school assumes $[\text{OH}^-]=0.150$ and obtains $1.13\times10^{-2}$. That approximation is poor here, because $2s$ is about 12–15% of 0.150.*

questions.question: Barium hydroxide is much less soluble in 0.150 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide solution than in pure water. Account for this difference.
questions.answer: This is the **common ion effect**. The NaOH solution already contains $\text{OH}^-$ ions. For $\text{Ba(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)$, Le Chatelier's principle predicts that the extra $\text{OH}^-$ shifts the equilibrium to the left, so less solid dissolves before $[\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$ reaches $K_{sp}$.

questions.question: Lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide solutions produce a bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide. If lead(II) iodide is "insoluble" in this reaction, explain why it appears on the HSC data sheet with a solubility constant of $9.8\times10^{-9}$.
questions.answer: No ionic solid is completely insoluble. Lead(II) iodide is **sparingly soluble**: a very small amount dissolves, establishing the equilibrium $\text{PbI}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Pb}^{2+}+2\text{I}^-$, and $K_{sp}$ measures its extent. In the demonstration the ion concentrations are high, so the ionic product greatly exceeds $K_{sp}$ and most of the lead(II) iodide precipitates.

questions.question: Acid theories have changed over time. Explain why theories change, referring to two specific examples of acid theories.
questions.answer:
A scientific theory is an explanation that accounts for current observations and makes testable predictions. It is revised or replaced when new evidence or technology produces observations it cannot explain.

**Arrhenius** proposed that acids ionise in water to produce $\text{H}^+$ ions and bases produce $\text{OH}^-$ ions. This explained neutralisation and differences in acid strength, but only applied to aqueous solutions and could not explain why substances such as $\text{NH}_3$ (with no OH) are basic, or why some salt solutions are acidic or basic.

**Brønsted and Lowry** therefore redefined an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor. This covers ammonia, reactions without water (such as $\text{HCl}(g)+\text{NH}_3(g)$), amphiprotic species, conjugate pairs and hydrolysis of salts.

The newer theory was adopted because it explained everything the older one did and also the observations the older one could not, while still having its own limits (it cannot explain acidic oxides reacting with basic oxides without proton transfer).

questions.question: A chemist determined the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in a bird's eggshell. The shell was dried, crushed and weighed (1.25 g). 25.00 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl was added to the eggshell until it had reacted. Phenolphthalein was added and the excess acid was titrated with 0.500 mol L⁻¹ NaOH; the average titre was 12.55 mL. Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the eggshell.
questions.answer:
Excess HCl $=n(\text{NaOH})=0.500\times0.01255=6.275\times10^{-3}$ mol.

HCl reacted with the shell $=0.02500-0.006275=0.018725$ mol.

$\text{CaCO}_3+2\text{HCl}\to\text{CaCl}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$, so $n(\text{CaCO}_3)=9.363\times10^{-3}$ mol.

$m=9.363\times10^{-3}\times100.09=0.937$ g, so the percentage is $\dfrac{0.937}{1.25}\times100=75.0\%$.

questions.question: The eggshell of a bird was analysed and found to contain 75.0% calcium carbonate by mass. The normal healthy range for this species is 85–93%. A biologist was worried that pollution was making the eggshells too thin. Explain whether the biologist was correct to be concerned.
questions.answer: Yes. At 75.0%, the calcium carbonate content is well below the healthy range of 85–93%, which indicates weaker, poorer-quality shells that could reduce the chicks' chance of survival. (More samples should be analysed to confirm that this egg is typical.)

questions.question: Explain how acid–base indicators work.
questions.answer:
An indicator is a weak acid whose molecule and conjugate base have different colours:
$$\text{HIn}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{In}^-(aq)$$

In acidic solution the high $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ shifts the equilibrium left, so the colour of HIn is seen. In basic solution $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, shifting the equilibrium right, so the colour of $\text{In}^-$ is seen. The colour changes over a pH range around the indicator's $\text{p}K_a$.

questions.question: Carbonic acid is a weak acid ($\text{p}K_a=6.377$ at 298 K). Calculate the pH of a 0.400 mol L⁻¹ solution of carbonic acid at 298 K.
questions.answer:
$K_a=10^{-6.377}=4.20\times10^{-7}$. For $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{HCO}_3^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$:

$$[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=\sqrt{4.20\times10^{-7}\times0.400}=4.10\times10^{-4},\qquad\text{pH}=3.39$$

*Note: the paper omitted the concentration in this part; its solution used 0.400 mol L⁻¹, which has been added to the question.*

questions.question: The carbonic acid–hydrogencarbonate buffer system is important in natural systems. Carbonic acid has $\text{p}K_a=6.377$ at 298 K. Calculate the pH of a buffer containing 0.400 mol L⁻¹ carbonic acid and 0.300 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydrogencarbonate.
questions.answer:
$$\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a+\log\frac{[\text{HCO}_3^-]}{[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3]}=6.377+\log\frac{0.300}{0.400}=6.25$$

*Note: the paper said "sodium carbonate", but its solution (and the buffer described) treats the salt as sodium hydrogencarbonate; the wording has been corrected. Actual $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ would react with the carbonic acid and give a different pH.*

questions.question:
Boiling points of some alkenes, amines and carboxylic acids:

| Alkene | M (g mol⁻¹) | b.p. (°C) | Amine | M | b.p. | Acid | M | b.p. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | | methanoic | 46 | 101 |
| | | | ethylamine | 45.1 | 17 | ethanoic | 60.1 | 118 |
| propene | 42.1 | −47 | 1-propylamine | 59.1 | 49 | propanoic | 74.1 | 141 |
| but-1-ene | 56.1 | −6 | 1-butylamine | 73.1 | 78 | butanoic | 88.1 | 164 |
| pent-1-ene | 70.1 | 30 | 1-pentanamine | 87.2 | 104 | | | |
| hex-1-ene | 84.2 | 64 | | | | | | |

Graph boiling point against molar mass, drawing a separate line for each of the three types of compound.
questions.answer: Put molar mass on the horizontal axis and boiling point on the vertical axis, with units, a title, a linear scale including negative temperatures, a line of best fit for each series and a key (see graph).

questions.question:
Boiling points of some alkenes, amines and carboxylic acids:

| Alkene | M (g mol⁻¹) | b.p. (°C) | Amine | M | b.p. | Acid | M | b.p. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | | methanoic | 46 | 101 |
| | | | ethylamine | 45.1 | 17 | ethanoic | 60.1 | 118 |
| propene | 42.1 | −47 | 1-propylamine | 59.1 | 49 | propanoic | 74.1 | 141 |
| but-1-ene | 56.1 | −6 | 1-butylamine | 73.1 | 78 | butanoic | 88.1 | 164 |
| pent-1-ene | 70.1 | 30 | 1-pentanamine | 87.2 | 104 | | | |
| hex-1-ene | 84.2 | 64 | | | | | | |

Explain the trends in boiling point shown by this data.
questions.answer:
Within each series, boiling point increases with molar mass: longer molecules have more electrons and a larger surface area, so dispersion forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.

At similar molar mass, acids > amines > alkenes. Alkenes are essentially non-polar and have only dispersion forces. Primary amines have polar N–H bonds, so they also form hydrogen bonds. Carboxylic acids have both a polar C=O and an O–H group; the O–H hydrogen bond is stronger than the N–H one and the molecules can pair up with two hydrogen bonds (dimers), so they have the highest boiling points.

questions.question: Describe a chemical test that would distinguish between propan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), butan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$). Include how you would do the test and the results used to identify each.
questions.answer:
Add a few mL of each alcohol to separate flasks containing acidified potassium dichromate solution and heat under reflux.

- **2-methylpropan-2-ol** (tertiary) is not oxidised: the solution stays orange.
- The other two turn the solution from orange ($\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$) to green ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$).

Distil off the organic product from each of these and add sodium carbonate solution:

- **propan-1-ol** (primary) is oxidised to propanoic acid, which produces bubbles of $\text{CO}_2$.
- **butan-2-ol** (secondary) is oxidised to butanone, which gives no bubbles.

*Note: the paper's drawing of the third alcohol labelled its central carbon "CH" while also bonding four groups to it; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is intended.*

questions.question: Soaps and detergents are very important chemicals in daily life. Explain how soap cleans dirt off clothes.
questions.answer:
A soap anion has a long non-polar hydrocarbon tail (hydrophobic) and a charged carboxylate head (hydrophilic).

The tails dissolve into the non-polar grease or dirt through dispersion forces, while the heads remain in the water, attracted by ion–dipole forces. Agitation lifts the grease from the fabric and breaks it into droplets surrounded by soap anions (micelles). The negatively charged surfaces repel each other, so the droplets stay suspended as an emulsion and are rinsed away.

questions.question: Many people in Australia only have access to bore water, which is hard water. Explain why it is better for them to use detergent-based cleaners rather than soap, including a relevant equation.
questions.answer:
Hard water contains $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions, which react with soap anions to form an insoluble precipitate (scum), removing soap from solution so it cannot clean:
$$2\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{35}\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)\to(\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{35}\text{COO})_2\text{Mg}(s)$$

Synthetic detergents do not form such precipitates: cationic detergents have positive heads, non-ionic detergents have no charge, and the sulfonate or sulfate heads of anionic detergents form much more soluble calcium and magnesium salts. They therefore keep working in hard water.

questions.question: Esterification is usually carried out by heating a carboxylic acid and an alcohol under reflux with concentrated sulfuric acid. Explain what would happen if there were no reflux apparatus.
questions.answer:
The mixture must be heated to react at a reasonable rate, but the alcohol, ester and some acid are volatile. Without a condenser to return the vapours to the flask they would escape, lowering the yield and creating a fire and inhalation hazard. Without heating, the reaction would be very slow.

*Note: the school states that esterification would not occur without reflux; it would still occur, but with loss of material (or very slowly without heat).*

questions.question: Explain what would happen in an esterification reaction if no concentrated sulfuric acid were added.
questions.answer: The reaction would be very slow, because sulfuric acid is the catalyst (it also absorbs water, which increases the yield).

questions.question:
The flowcharts show how unknown cations and anions can be identified. An unknown salt gave these results:

**Test 1** (cation solutions added): iron(II), no change; iron(III), no change; barium, white precipitate.

**Test 2** (anion solutions added): hydroxide, blue precipitate; chloride, no change; sulfate, no change.

Identify the salt.
questions.answer: Copper(II) sulfate: the white precipitate with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ (and none with iron ions) indicates sulfate, and the blue precipitate with hydroxide indicates $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.

questions.question:
The flowcharts show how unknown cations and anions can be identified. An unknown salt gave these results:

**Test 1** (cation solutions added): iron(II), no change; iron(III), no change; barium, white precipitate.

**Test 2** (anion solutions added): hydroxide, blue precipitate; chloride, no change; sulfate, no change.

Write the net ionic equations for the two positive results.

$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)\to\text{BaSO}_4(s)$$
$$\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\to\text{Cu(OH)}_2(s)$$

questions.question: A chemist determined the amount of lead in soil using atomic absorption spectroscopy, using the calibration curve shown. A 2.00 g sample of soil was dissolved in acid and diluted to 50.00 mL. The absorbance of this solution was 0.20. Calculate the concentration of lead ions in the sample solution in mg L⁻¹.
questions.answer:
From the curve, $A=0.20$ corresponds to $c\approx1.4\times10^{-5}$ mol L⁻¹.

$$c=1.4\times10^{-5}\times207.2=2.9\times10^{-3}\ \text{g L}^{-1}=2.9\ \text{mg L}^{-1}$$

*Note: the paper asked for the concentration "in the soil in mg L⁻¹", but 2.9 mg L⁻¹ (the school's answer) is the concentration of the prepared solution, as now worded. For the soil itself: 50 mL holds about 0.15 mg of lead per 2.00 g, about 73 mg kg⁻¹.*

questions.question: Calculate the concentration (mol L⁻¹) of a copper sulfate solution analysed in a colorimeter: light of 635 nm entering the sample $I_0=40$ cd; light reaching the detector $I=20$ cd; path length 1 cm; molar absorption coefficient $\varepsilon=2.81\ \text{M}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$.

A chemist ran a full spectrum scan with a UV–visible spectrophotometer of sunscreens with SPF 15, 30 and 50 (Diagram 1). Diagram 2 shows part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Write a conclusion that can be drawn from Diagram 1 only.
questions.answer: The higher the SPF rating, the greater the absorbance across the wavelengths scanned (220–400 nm).

questions.question: A chemist ran a full spectrum scan with a UV–visible spectrophotometer of sunscreens with SPF 15, 30 and 50 (Diagram 1). Diagram 2 shows part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Write a conclusion that can be drawn from Diagrams 1 and 2 together.
questions.answer: The sunscreens absorb most strongly (about 240 nm) in the UVC region, with a second absorption peak (about 300 nm) in the UVB region, and absorb progressively less in the UVA region.

questions.question: A chemist ran a full spectrum scan with a UV–visible spectrophotometer of sunscreens with SPF 15, 30 and 50 (Diagram 1). Diagram 2 shows part of the electromagnetic spectrum. The chemist now wants to determine the concentration of the SPF chemical in a sunscreen. Outline what must be done after the full spectrum scan to find this concentration with the UV–visible spectrophotometer.
questions.answer:
1. Choose the wavelength of maximum absorbance (about 240 nm) and set the instrument to it.
2. Prepare several standard solutions of the pure SPF chemical of known concentration, and a blank.
3. Measure their absorbances and plot a calibration curve.
4. Dissolve and dilute a known amount of the sunscreen, measure its absorbance under the same conditions, read its concentration from the curve and correct for the dilution.

questions.question: Compare atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS), colorimetry and UV–visible spectrophotometry.
questions.answer:
All three measure how much light a sample absorbs and, using the Beer–Lambert law and a calibration curve, determine concentration. They differ as follows.

| Feature | AAS | Colorimetry | UV–visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light source | hollow cathode lamp of the element being measured | visible lamp (tungsten or LED) | deuterium (UV) and tungsten (visible) lamps |
| Sample | solution sprayed into a flame, forming free atoms | coloured solution in a cuvette | solution in a cuvette |
| Species analysed | metals, even at ppm levels or below | coloured species (or those made coloured) | species absorbing UV or visible light, organic and inorganic |
| Wavelength | the element's own lines, highly specific | a filter giving a broad band of the complementary colour | monochromator; can scan a whole spectrum |
| Use | quantitative | quantitative | quantitative, and some qualitative identification |
